title: Investigating the TASK1 potassium channel in equine atrial myocardium as a potential treatment target for atrial fibrillation.
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common clinically relevant arrhythmia in horses, with limited pharmacological treatment options in both veterinary and human medicine. TASK1 potassium channels represent a promising atrial-selective antiarrhythmic target, but their relevance in horses has not been established. To characterize equine TASK1 (eqTASK1) channels regarding structural conservation, electrophysiological function, pharmacological sensitivity, cardiac expression pattern and in vivo electrophysiological effects of TASK1 inhibition. Sixteen horses killed for non-cardiovascular reasons, of which 10 horses used for tissue harvesting and six horses for in vivo testing. Functional and pharmacological properties of eq TASK1 and human (hTASK1) channels were assessed in Xenopus laevis oocytes using two-electrode voltage clamp recordings. Cardiac expression of eqTASK1 was analysed by qRT-PCR and immunoblotting, while in vivo electrophysiological studies were performed in anaesthetized horses before and after intravenous ketodoxapram administration. EqTASK1 and h TASK1 channels demonstrated high structural conservation, comparable potassium-selective background currents and preserved pharmacological sensitivity with species-dependent differences in potency. EqTASK1 expression was strongly enriched in atrial and nodal tissue, whereas ventricular expression was minimal. In vivo administration of ketodoxapram significantly prolonged atrial effective refractory periods from 275 ± 54 to 418 ± 94 ms without significant changes in heart rate or atrioventricular conduction parameters. EqTASK1 channels are highly conserved with human orthologs and display pronounced atrial-predominant cardiac expression. In vivo TASK1 inhibition prolongs atrial refractoriness in horses, supporting TASK1 as a translational atrial-selective antiarrhythmic target in both human and veterinary medicine.

title: Large-scale energy infrastructure projects and thoroughbred stud farms: equine welfare, evidence gaps and planning considerations.
abstract: Industrial-scale renewable energy developments i.e. solar photovoltaic (PV) installations and wind energy facilities, form a central component of Ireland's national decarbonisation strategy. As these infrastructures expand, they are increasingly being proposed or developed within rural regions that also contain high densities of Thoroughbred breeding establishments. This creates a potential interface between national energy policy, rural land use, equine welfare and the operational requirements of the Thoroughbred industry which is of national and international importance.Direct empirical evidence examining the effects of large-scale renewable energy developments on Thoroughbred mares, foals and youngstock on adjacent stud farms remains limited. However, established evidence from equine sensory physiology, behavioural science, veterinary medicine and environmental studies demonstrates that horses are highly responsive to noise, visual stimuli, airborne particulates and sudden environmental disturbance. These findings provide biologically plausible pathways through which construction and, in some circumstances, operation of large-scale energy infrastructure may adversely affect equine behaviour, health and welfare.Current Irish planning legislation does not specifically require equine welfare considerations to be incorporated into decision-making for developments adjacent to breeding establishments. This commentary argues that the absence of direct equine-specific evidence should not be interpreted as evidence of absence of risk. Rather, it supports a proportionate and precautionary approach incorporating equine-specific assessment, independent veterinary input, appropriate mitigation and site-specific planning where major renewable energy infrastructure is proposed in close proximity to stud farms.

title: Deep learning-based differentiation of FLASH ultrasound windows.
abstract: Equine colic emergencies present highly stressful, time-critical scenarios for both clinicians and patients, thus rapid and accurate diagnostic triage is paramount. To support veterinarians under these high-pressure conditions, deep learning tools can be leveraged for automated image recognition to assist in localizing abdominal organs and interpreting FLASH (Fast Localized Abdominal Sonography of Horses) ultrasound windows. A software tool was developed to identify FLASH-specific ultrasound windows on the equine abdomen and to recognize ultrasonographic organ patterns. Retrospective-prospective comparison of software and clinical examination, model development. A deep learning approach for image classification was used to train software to assign ultrasound images to FLASH windows. Strongest software performance was observed for the duodenal window, with all test images correctly classified, corresponding to a recall of 1.00. Nephrosplenic window demonstrated high classification accuracy, but 23% of images were misclassified as gastric window. While 84% of ventral images were correctly classified, 16% were predicted as duodenal window. Most pronounced confusion was observed between ventral and thoracic windows, with only 55% of thoracic images correctly identified. Left and right middle third FLASH windows 4 and 6 were substantially underrepresented and were therefore excluded from further analyses. In addition, these windows exhibited high anatomical similarity, which further complicated their differentiation. Sources of selection bias was interpretation of windows and the definition of normal physiological ultrasound images by the examiners. The specific FLASH windows were not homogeneously dispersed in the dataset (e.g., FLASH windows 4 and 6 were underrepresented). The developed deep learning tool demonstrates the feasibility of automated recognition of standardized equine FLASH windows and may support ultrasound training as an educational aid for first-day competencies. Future incorporation of organ-level annotations and probe position information may improve discrimination between anatomically similar windows and enhance model performance.

title: In vitro anthelmintic activity of the monoterpene linalool, alone and combined with the nematophagous fungus Duddingtonia flagrans, in the control of gastrointestinal nematodes in horses.
abstract: This study evaluated, in vitro, the anthelmintic activity of the monoterpene linalool, alone and in association with the fungus Duddingtonia flagrans, against gastrointestinal nematodes of horses. Nematodes from the superfamily Strongyloidea, obtained from naturally infected horses, were used. The ovicidal activity of linalool was evaluated using the Egg Hatch Test (EHT). The larvicidal activity was evaluated using the Larval Motility Inhibition Test (LMIT), in which infective larvae (L3) were assigned to experimental groups treated with linalool alone (0.15, 0.3, 0.6, 1.25, 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 40, and 80 mg/mL), D. flagrans conidia alone (100,000, 500,000, and 1,000,000 conidia), or the combination of both. In the EHT, linalool completely inhibited egg hatching (100%) at all concentrations of 0.25 mg/mL and above, with an LC₅₀ of 0.15 mg/mL (0.015%). In the LMIT, linalool completely inhibited larval motility (100%) at all concentrations of 0.5 mg/mL and above, with an LC₅₀ of 0.103 mg/mL (0.010%). The association with the fungus D. flagrans promoted a significant reduction (p ≤ 0.05) in the number of live larvae after 72 h, reaching 100% inhibition within 14 days. The groups treated only with conidia showed lower efficacy, whereas the association with linalool enhanced the antiparasitic effect without impairing trap formation or the predatory capacity of the fungus. Thus, the results demonstrated that linalool has relevant ovicidal and larvicidal activity, and that its association with D. flagrans constitutes a promising alternative for the biological control of helminth infections in horses.

title: Microsecond Barrier-Crossing Collapse in Cytochrome c Folding Revealed by Two-Dimensional Fluorescence Lifetime Correlation Spectroscopy.
journal: The journal of physical chemistry letters
abstract: Protein folding is initiated with a volume contraction called collapse. While the microsecond collapse of horse cyt c has been intensely studied, its molecular mechanism remains elusive. To characterize the structural change, we prepared three cyt c variants labeled with a fluorescent dye at distinct sites (D50, A83, and E104). We track their dynamics via FRET between the dye and the heme by two-dimensional fluorescence lifetime correlation spectroscopy (2D FLCS), which has single-molecule sensitivity and sub-microsecond time resolution. The results reveal that the collapse exhibits two-state dynamics between structurally distributed ensembles, occurring on a time scale of tens of microseconds across all variants. This indicates a global contraction of the whole protein structure with a substantial free energy barrier. A slight delay observed for the D50 variant suggests the late folding of its associated loop. This study demonstrates the capability of 2D FLCS to characterize a small free-energy barrier in complex biophysical processes.

title: Study on the Methyl Viologen-Mediated Electrochemical Reduction of Coenzyme NAD+ in the Triton X-100-Stabilized Methyl tert-Butyl Ether-in-H2O Microemulsion.
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: An oil-in-water microemulsion is an excellent candidate medium for the electrochemical regeneration of the coenzyme NADH and its subsequent coupled conversion application due to its good electrical conductivity and solubilization capacity for hydrophobic substrates. In this work, the reduced methyl viologen (MV+•)-mediated electrochemical reduction of coenzyme NAD+ was studied in a Triton X-100 (TX-100)-stabilized methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE)-in-water microemulsion. The effects of the surfactant concentration and the oil content on the electrochemical behavior of the MV2+/MV+• couple and the activity of diaphorase (DH) were systematically investigated. The results show that in the microemulsion, the couple exhibits excellent reversibility. Compared with the aqueous buffer system, the couple in the microemulsion system has a more positive formal potential and a lower redox peak current, depending on the levels of both the surfactant and the oil. The positive shift of the formal potential is attributed to the stabilizing effect of the surfactant aggregates on the relatively hydrophobic MV+• species, and the decrease of the redox currents is ascribed to the decrease of the electroactive area of the electrode due to the adsorption of the surfactant and the oil as well as the decrease of the diffusion coefficients of MV species associated with or solubilized in the surfactant aggregates. The activity of DH in the microemulsion system also depends on the TX-100 concentration and the MTBE content. Increases in both [TX-100] and [MTBE] result in a decrease in DH activity. This phenomenon could be explained based on the [TX-100]/[MTBE]-dependent changes in the local acidity and the local concentration of the substrate DCPIP in the microemulsions. Based on cyclic voltammetry, the MV+•-mediated electroreduction of NAD+ in the TX-100-stabilized MTBE/H2O (0.1 M PB, pH = 7.0) microemulsion was studied. For the microemulsion system containing 0.5 mM MV2+, 5 mM NAD+, and 26.6 μM DH, when a scan rate of 2 mV s-1 was applied, a typical steady-state S-shaped CV curve was obtained. UV-vis spectroscopy confirms that the NADH generated by the mediated reaction is bioactive. By coupling the MV+•-mediated NADH electrochemical regeneration reaction with the horse liver alcohol dehydrogenase (HLADH)-catalyzed reduction of the hydrophobic substrate 4-phenyl-2-butanone, the enantiomerically pure (S)-4-phenyl-2-butanol can be selectively obtained. After 12 h, the yield of the product in the microemulsion is approximately 10 times that in the DMSO-buffer mixed homogeneous system. This difference in yield is caused by the differences in enzyme activity and stability, as well as in the substrate local concentration and reactivity in the two systems. The present study indicates that the TX-100-stabilized MTBE-in-water microemulsion is a suitable medium for the electrochemical regeneration of NADH and the electroenzymatic conversion of water-insoluble substrates catalyzed by NADH-dependent oxidoreductases.

title: New World screwworm in livestock production systems: biosecurity, economic considerations, and management for cattle, sheep, goat, horse, and swine producers.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) is a transboundary obligate myiasis-causing parasite that poses serious threats to livestock production through infestation of living tissue, rapid lesion progression, animal suffering, and substantial economic loss. Between June 3 and June 16, 2026, the US confirmed 12 cases of New World screwworm in domestic animals across Texas and New Mexico, marking the first detections in production livestock in the continental US since 1966. Cases have involved cattle, sheep, goats, and a dog across multiple counties, with all 12 classified as active and no wild fly trap detections recorded as of the manuscript preparation date. This narrative review synthesizes current producer-facing evidence on production-level risk factors, herd and flock biosecurity, species-specific vulnerabilities, surveillance and reporting pathways, and the economic and trade implications of an active outbreak. Practical prevention measures examined include timing invasive husbandry procedures to low-risk periods, strengthening wound prevention and inspection protocols, and improving sanitation for vehicles, equipment, and personnel. Population-level control strategies (principally the sterile insect technique, now deployed via aerial and ground releases in and around the detection zone) and current regulatory responses, including multiple FDA emergency-use authorizations for animal drugs, are summarized to support preparedness planning across livestock systems. The principal contribution of this review is to reframe the producer and veterinary response to screwworm from individual-animal treatment to production-system prevention, consolidating 2023 to 2026 guidance from USDA, FDA, AVMA, and cooperative extension programs into a practical roadmap for reducing risk, preserving animal welfare, and protecting market access at the herd and flock level.

title: erm(46) copy number determines macrolide resistance in Rhodococcus equi.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: To develop a multiplex real-time PCR assay for simultaneous detection of Rhodococcus equi (choE), virulence (vapA), and macrolide-resistance determinants (erm[46], erm[51]), and evaluate their clinical and temporal trends. Clinical R equi isolates (n = 229) obtained from the Hagyard Equine Medical Institute laboratory were collected sequentially over a 3-year surveillance period (2021 to 2023) from 14 states and underwent broth microdilution susceptibility testing. A cohort of 214 isolates with high-quality DNA was characterized using quantitative PCR. Geographic distribution, seasonal trends, and genotypic-phenotypic concordance were evaluated. The multiplex PCR assay demonstrated 100% analytical specificity. The virulence gene vapA was present in 94.4% (202 of 214) of isolates. The macrolide resistance determinant erm(46) was highly prevalent at 62.6% (134 of 214), showing a significant seasonal increase during July to December periods at 76.6% (vs 58.2% in January to June). Crucially, erm(51) was detected in a single isolate (0.5%), representing its first recorded clinical identification in R equi. Unstratified genotypic-phenotypic agreement for macrolides was fair (κ = 0.22 to 0.25). However, stratification by genomic copy number revealed near-perfect concordance (κ ≥ 0.97) exclusively among isolates harboring > 50,000 target copies. Alternative agents (gentamicin, ceftiofur, minocycline, doxycycline) maintained 97% to 100% susceptibility, regardless of erm(46) status. While erm(46) is widely distributed across R equi-endemic farms, actual phenotypic resistance expression is strongly copy-number dependent. The clinical emergence of erm(51) expands the known resistome of this pathogen. Incorporating quantitative molecular screening into routine R equi diagnostics provides crucial real-time therapeutic guidance, supporting precision medicine and targeted antimicrobial stewardship on endemic equine farms.

title: Auscultation for pre-exercise screening in the horse.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: To describe the highlights of cardiac auscultation of the equine athlete in the context of pre-exercise screening for cardiac adverse event prevention. Horses. Tutorial description. Description of the highlights of cardiac auscultation of the equine athlete in the context of pre-exercise screening for cardiac adverse event and exercise-associated sudden death prevention. Cardiac adverse events and exercise-associated deaths are problems that affect horses' health, riders' safety, and the public perception of welfare during equestrian sports. Screening before participation in sports has helped decrease the incidence of sudden death in humans. We believe auscultation may be a high-yield, low-cost strategy to improve equine welfare and a key component of a prevention program for exercise-associated sudden death in equine athletes. What we describe here highlights that an irregularly irregular rhythm is atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise and is the main target of pre-exercise auscultation. Concerning murmurs are the second target; multiple examples of audio, video, and electrocardiograms are shown.

title: Infracyanine green photodynamic therapy provides short-term disease control, but recurrence is common in equine immune-mediated keratitis.
abstract: To evaluate long-term clinical outcomes, recurrence rates, and complications following photodynamic therapy (PDT) in horses with immune-mediated keratitis. Medical records of horses treated with PDT at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences Equine Clinic from May 2018 through October 2025 were reviewed retrospectively. Eyes with a clinical diagnosis of recurrent immune-mediated keratitis that had responded to immunosuppressive therapy and been subjected to PDT therapy were included. Infracyanine green was injected intrastromally, followed by irradiation with an 810-nm diode laser. Recurrence, postoperative complications, and follow-up duration were recorded. Recurrence-free survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis, and associations with recurrence were explored. 30 eyes from 28 horses were included. Recurrence occurred in 18 of 30 eyes (60.0%); 12 of 30 (40.0%) remained recurrence-free without medication at final follow-up (median, 1,849 days). Recurrence-free survival was 83.1% at 1 year (95% CI, 64.0% to 92.6%) and 49.8% at 2 years (95% CI, 30.2% to 66.6%); median recurrence-free time was 693 days. Postoperative epithelial defects occurred in 22 of 30 eyes (73.3%), and secondary bacterial ulcerative keratitis developed in 4 of 30 (13.3%); all ulcers healed after adjusted treatment. No clear associations between evaluated variables and recurrence were detected. PDT provided medication-free disease control in some eyes, particularly during the first postoperative year, but recurrence was common with longer follow-up. Epithelial defects were frequent, although all resolved without major sequelae. PDT may be useful when prolonged topical treatment is impractical; repeated early fluorescein staining and long-term surveillance are recommended.

title: Intravenous regional limb perfusion techniques in the anesthetized foal.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: To provide a video tutorial on how to perform IV regional limb perfusion (IVRLP) using the cephalic or saphenous vein in anesthetized foals. Foals from neonatal to weaning age not amenable to standing, sedated procedures. A pneumatic or wide-rubber tourniquet is applied around the proximal antebrachium or gaskin. The IVRLP dose of desired antimicrobial is diluted with physiologic saline to 30 mL of total volume. A 23-gauge winged infusion set or 22-gauge, 1-inch IV catheter is inserted into either the cephalic or saphenous vein distal to the tourniquet, and the entire perfusate volume is administered slowly by hand or with a syringe pump. The needle or catheter is removed, a pressure bandage applied over the venipuncture site, and the tourniquet left in place for a minimum of 20 minutes and up to 30 minutes. When IVRLP is administered in conjunction with systemic antimicrobial administration, the dose administered via IVRLP should be subtracted from the total systemic dose to avoid systemic toxicity. When combined with systemic administration, cephalic or saphenous IVRLP in the anesthetized foal is considered an effective technique for achieving adequate systemic antimicrobial concentrations and supraphysiologic antimicrobial concentrations in the tissues and synovial compartments of the limbs. While IVRLP in foals is commonly performed in equine practice, appropriate technique is essential to maximize the clinical effect. This tutorial video is intended to provide practitioners with basic instruction for proper technique of IVRLP using the cephalic or saphenous vein in the anesthetized foal.

title: Co-contamination of aquatic food animals by microplastics, heavy metals, and pesticides: bioaccumulation, human health risk, and role of artificial intelligence.
abstract: Aquatic food animals provide essential proteins, omega-3 fatty acids, and micronutrients to billions of people worldwide, yet their safety is increasingly challenged by the co-occurrence of microplastics (MPs), heavy metals (HMs), and pesticides in aquatic ecosystems. Unlike previous reviews that examine these contaminant classes separately, this review presents an integrated framework linking contamination sources, bioaccumulation, trophic transfer, human health risks, food security, and regulatory responses. MPs can act as physicochemical vectors by adsorbing HMs and pesticides and releasing them following gastrointestinal desorption (the Trojan horse mechanism), although the importance of this pathway depends on polymer characteristics, weathering, gut conditions, and ambient contaminant concentrations. Co-exposure may produce synergistic, additive, or antagonistic effects depending on contaminant combinations, exposure conditions, and biological endpoints, highlighting that synergism should not be assumed universally. Human health risk assessment indices are evaluated alongside international regulatory guidance, with emphasis on their limitations as screening-level tools that do not account for contaminant interactions and are sensitive to exposure assumptions. The implications of co-contamination for all four FAO pillars of food security are examined through regional case studies of seafood-dependent populations. Machine learning and explainable AI applications for contaminant detection, environmental monitoring, and bioaccumulation prediction are evaluated and compared across four application domains, distinguishing proof-of-concept studies from regulatory-ready applications. Finally, key research priorities, including mixture toxicology, standardized nanoplastic analysis, long-term biomonitoring in data-sparse regions, and robust ML model validation, are identified to support future research and evidence-based seafood safety governance.

title: Left Ventricular Volume Indexing in Athletic Brazilian Sport Horses Using Body Weight.
abstract: Left ventricular (LV) volume assessment evaluates cardiac size and remodelling in horses. Single-plane Simpson method of discs (SMOD) provides volumetric measurements requiring body size normalization. We described LV volumes using SMOD in healthy Brazilian Sport Horses (BH) and evaluated thoracic-girth-estimated body weight (BWe) versus scale-measured weight (BWs) for indexing. Thirty BH horses (15 males, 15 females; 4-16 years) underwent echocardiography. LV end-diastolic (LVEDV), end-systolic volumes (LVESV), and ejection fraction (EF%) were obtained using SMOD. Body weight was scale-measured and estimated via thoracic girth formula. Volumes were indexed to BWs, BWe, and a 500-kg reference. Mean LVEDV was 1060 ± 154 mL (95% CI: 1003-1118), LVESV 318 ± 77 mL (95% CI: 290-347), and EF 70.0 ± 5.4%. Overall, BWe was associated with BWs (R² = 0.61; P < 0.0001) with mean bias of +33.25 kg (limits of agreement: -37.59 to +104.09 kg), mean absolute error of 39 ± 28.83 kg, and percentage error of 8.92 ± 7.27%. LVEDV/BWs averaged 2.30 ± 0.29 mL/kg and LVEDV/BWe 2.15 ± 0.26 mL/kg. Normalization to 500 kg yielded LVEDV[500] of 1151 ± 146 and 1069 ± 131 mL, and LVESV[500] of 346 ± 83 and 321 ± 70 mL (BWs; BWe). Indexed variables showed moderate to strong linear association between methods. In this sample, no sex or age differences were detected. Body weight normalization improved interindividual comparability. While BWe offers a practical field alternative, estimation errors warrant caution in individual evaluations, making BWs preferred.

title: Factors associated with embryo recovery in mares: A retrospective multicenter analysis and practical overview of embryo flushing protocols.
abstract: Embryo recovery (ER) is a major determinant of efficiency in equine embryo-transfer programs and may be influenced by biological, management, and technical factors. This retrospective multicenter study aimed to identify factors associated with positive ER and to describe the embryo-flushing (EF) techniques used in three commercial embryo-transfer programs. We hypothesized that factors associated with ER would differ among clinics because of differences in mare populations, semen types, management practices, and flushing systems. The study included 2861 EF cycles: 465 cycles from 196 mares in Clinic 1, 661 cycles from 265 mares in Clinic 2, and 1735 cycles from 277 mares in Clinic 3. Factors associated with positive ER were evaluated separately for each clinic using multivariable generalized linear mixed models, with mare identity included as a random intercept. Additional univariable analyses were used to examine selected factors individually. Overall ER was 55.7%, 51.4%, and 73.5% in Clinics 1, 2, and 3, respectively. In the multivariable analyses, none of the evaluated fixed effects were significantly associated with ER in Clinic 1. In Clinic 2, semen type was the only significant fixed effect, with greater odds of ER using chilled than frozen semen (OR = 2.07, 95% CI: 1.37-3.11; p < 0.001). Clinic 3 used fresh semen exclusively, and donor mare age was the only significant fixed effect, with the odds of ER decreasing by 9% for each additional year of age (OR = 0.91, 95% CI: 0.88-0.94; p < 0.001). Although the overall effect of season phase was not significant in Clinic 3, ER was lower during mid-season than early season (OR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.46-0.99; p = 0.043). Mare identity had a significant random effect in all three clinics (p ≤ 0.05), indicating substantial between-mare variability. Repeated EF within the same season did not reduce ER in any clinic, including among mares undergoing four or more cycles. In the additional analyses, multiple ovulation was associated with higher ER in Clinics 1 and 3 but not in Clinic 2. In Clinic 2, experienced operators showed a tendency toward higher ER than less experienced operators (52.4% vs. 37.7%; p = 0.06). In conclusion, factors associated with ER differed among clinical settings. The consistent mare effect, the absence of a decline in ER with repeated flushing, and the potential influence of operator experience emphasize the importance of individual mare fertility and clinic-specific management when evaluating the efficiency of commercial embryo-transfer programs.

title: A Selective Bis-Catecholate Siderophore-Ampicillin Conjugate Expands Activity against Multidrug-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a global public health crisis, with multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa among the most critical threats. The high cost and slow pace of novel antibiotic development, coupled with rapid resistance evolution, demand innovative strategies. Here, we present a Trojan horse approach using siderophore-antibiotic conjugates (SACs) to hijack bacterial iron uptake systems and deliver β-lactam payloads across the Gram-negative outer membrane. We designed a series of ampicillin conjugates with mono-catecholate, bis-catecholate, and catecholate-hydroxamate siderophores. These conjugates demonstrate potent antimicrobial activity. Notably, the lead compound, BC-2-Amp, shows broad-spectrum and highly selective activity against a panel of 105 clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that BC-2-Amp utilizes PiuA as a critical receptor for targeted delivery. Complementary in vivo experiments further confirmed its promising therapeutic efficacy. Collectively, these findings establish SACs as a potent strategy for broadening the spectrum of β-lactam antibiotics and provide a robust platform for high-potency drug delivery.

title: Fluorescent tagging for assessment of environmental cleaning in an equine hospital.
abstract: Healthcare-associated infections increase morbidity, mortality, and treatment costs in both human and veterinary medicine, and environmental contamination can contribute to their occurrence. Monitoring of environmental cleaning is an important component of multimodal infection control strategies. Fluorescent tagging is a low-cost, practical approach that correlates with reduced environmental contamination in human and small animal hospitals. Its applicability in equine hospitals, where surface characteristics and contamination risks differ, has not yet been evaluated. To evaluate fluorescent tagging as a monitoring tool for environmental cleaning in an equine hospital, to assess the impact of active feedback, and to validate an objective ImageJ-based assessment against subjective evaluation. Before-after study. A commercial fluorescent dye was applied to surfaces in examination rooms and stalls. Fluorescent tag removal was evaluated visually and objectively using standardised photography and ImageJ-based green intensity analysis. Surfaces were sampled repeatedly across two study phases, separated by structured feedback to cleaning staff. Aerobic colony counts (ACC) were performed during phase II adjacent to fluorescent tags to assess bacterial contamination before and after cleaning. Objective ImageJ-based analysis accurately distinguished between removed, partially removed, and not removed fluorescent tags, and there was strong agreement with subjective visual assessment. In examination rooms, provision of feedback resulted in a significant overall improvement in cleaning efficacy, particularly in orthopaedic treatment rooms (room1: log-odds ratio = 1.71; q-value = 0.033, room2: log-odds ratio = 2.11; q-value = 0.01), whereas no improvement was observed in stables (q-value >0.05). The ACC were not associated with fluorescent tag removal grades (q-value >0.05). Subjective and objective assessments were performed by the same non-blinded examiner, single centre design and limited ACC assessment. Fluorescent tagging is a feasible monitoring method for assessing environmental cleaning efficacy in an equine hospital, and objective quantification correlated closely with subjective visual assessment. Active feedback improved cleaning performance in examination rooms but not in stables.

title: Arthropod-Related Health Threats (ARHTs) and Nuisance Arthropods in North Khorasan Province, Iran: A Comprehensive Review.
abstract: The arthropod vectors, such as mosquitoes, sand flies, and ticks, transmit various pathogens to humans and animals, leading to public health issues. Therefore, an effective disease surveillance system is essential to provide information on these diseases in order to monitor their trends worldwide. The current study focused on the prevalence of arthropod-borne diseases and their vectors in North Khorasan Province located in northeastern Iran, bordering Turkmenistan. A narrative literature review was conducted to analyze the status of arthropod-related health threats (ARHTs) and their vectors in this area. Sources with no time limit up to 2025 were examined from PubMed, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science databases using keywords like vector, arthropod, North Khorasan, and Iran. After excluding duplicates and irrelevant content, a final list of 31 papers was thoroughly evaluated. This province exhibits the occurrence of several major ARHTs, including visceral leishmaniasis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, West Nile fever, chikungunya, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, Q fever, Theileria infection, equine piroplasmosis, dirofilariasis, Dipylidium caninum infection, fascioliasis, hymenolepiasis, scorpionism, spider bites, pediculosis, and myiasis. Given the complex and diverse ecosystem of North Khorasan, implementing tailored and innovative strategies is essential for effective surveillance and early detection of arthropod-borne diseases, thus enabling timely and efficient management of these health threats.

title: Clonal articular cartilage progenitors outperform mesenchymal stromal cells in mitigating post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
abstract: This study aimed to compare the functional, pathological, and immunomodulatory properties of articular chondroprogenitors (ACPs) with those of bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) in preventing the progression of post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) after destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) injury in a mouse model. ACP and MSC were isolated from three horses and assessed for their immunomodulatory capacity in vitro. Aliquots of selected ACP clones and MSCs were injected intra-articularly into male mice 1-week post destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM). The functional mobility of the mice before the injury and at weeks 2, 4, and 8 post-injury was assessed by two methods: ANY-maze™ voluntary mobility monitoring and DigiGait™ compulsory gait analysis. Upon euthanasia, joints were collected for histological scoring. In vitro assessments demonstrated that ACPs and MSCs had anti-inflammatory properties: both treatments produced lower levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, while only the ACPs produced more anti-inflammatory cytokines than controls. In vivo, both ACPs and MSCs lessened the effects of DMM on mobility. Histological scoring revealed significant reductions of PTOA in the medial compartment with ACPs relative to both MSCs and vehicle controls. Overall, ACPs effectively reduced PTOA progression to a greater extent than MSCs. Our findings demonstrated that both equine ACP and MSC treatments provided symptom modification over vehicle controls in a short-term animal study. Notably, ACPs may be more efficacious than MSCs at reducing structural joint pathology.

title: Equine (Equus caballus) primary post-natal brain-derived cells: immortalization and preliminary reprogramming attempts to induced pluripotent stem cells.
abstract: Equines represent an underexplored yet highly relevant model for studying neurological diseases within a One Health framework. Here, we report the first establishment of post-natal equine brain-derived in vitro systems, including equine primary post-natal brain-derived cells (EpBCs) and their immortalized counterparts (EiBCs). EpBCs were isolated from the hippocampus and successfully expanded, while immortalization via Simian virus 40 large T antigen generated EiBCs lines with distinct transcriptomic reprogramming characterized by cell cycle activation and partial dedifferentiation. Despite testing three non-integrating approaches-Sendai virus, episomal vectors, and synthetic mRNA-no induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)-like colonies were detected under the tested conditions, possibly reflecting a combination of species-specific, cell-intrinsic, and donor-specific factors, as well as culture conditions, factor compatibility, and delivery efficiency. Together, these findings establish a foundational equine brain-derived cell platform and highlight key challenges in equine reprogramming. Its One Health relevance is prospective, as this system may support future comparative neurological research and the development of equine brain organoids.

title: Bioactivity profiling of linear venom peptides from Italian small wood-scorpion (Euscorpius italicus).
abstract: Rising host-expansion and the global spread of pest insects, confront agricultural sectors with substantial concerns. A promising source of potential lead compounds to target these growing challenges are animal venoms which abound with a huge diversity of bioactive peptides suited for both pest control and drug discovery. Arachnids in particular contribute substantially to the extreme diversity of highly adapted venom compounds, and for some of these, translational potential in pest control has already been demonstrated. Members of the Euscorpiidae family of scorpions are among the most successful groups of scorpions in Europe. Although they use their venom for hunting, none of their toxins has thus far been functionally evaluated as their low toxicity to humans has kept them out of the spotlight of venom research. We hypothesize that their venom peptides exert insecticidal activity which might be harnessed for pest control applications. Based on our hypothesis, we conducted bioactivity profiling of linear venom peptides derived from Euscorpius italicus, one of the most common euscorpiid species. In silico analyses revealed them as neutral to cationaic alpha helical peptides with high hydrophobicity. Functionally, our established profiling pipeline that combines in vivo and in vitro bioassays, reveals that one of the tested linear venom peptides, Ei1, causes mortality in Drosophila suzukii postinjection, as well as signs of neuroparalysis. Furthermore, Ei1 exhibits inhibitory effects on Staphylococcus aureus, while also affecting MDCK II cells and equine erythrocytes, implying functions in host defense. This study reveals insights on properties of Euscorpiidae venom, their ecological values for predation and defensive function against microbial colonization of the venom glands - revealing further knowledge to the growing biodiscovery of animal venoms and potential agricultural functions as a biological insecticide. © 2026 The Author(s). Pest Management Science published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd on behalf of Society of Chemical Industry.

title: EUCAST disk diffusion: Can Mueller-Hinton agar with 5% sheep blood (MH-S) be an alternative medium for fastidious organisms?
journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
abstract: EUCAST recommends Mueller-Hinton (MH) agar with defibrinated horse blood and β-NAD (MH-F) for disk diffusion testing of fastidious organisms, but MH-F has been difficult to access in several geographical areas. The objective of this study was to evaluate MH with sheep blood (MH-S) as an alternative medium. Disk diffusion (DD) was performed according to EUCAST recommendations on MH-F and MH-S in parallel. All species with breakpoints on MH-F agar were tested, except for Haemophilus influenzae due to its inadequate growth on MH-S. Growth and zone diameters from parallel tests on MH-F and MH-S were compared and categorical agreement was calculated according to EUCAST recommendations. Essential agreement and bias were calculated adapting the recommendations for MIC evaluations in ISO 20776-2. Also, zone diameter distributions on MH-S produced from MH agar from three manufacturers were compared. Growth on MH-S was equally good as on MH-F for all tested species. Correlation between DD results on MH-S and MH-F was good, with 61-85, 89-100 and 95-100% inhibition zone diameters within 1, 2 and 3 mm, respectively, for each species/organism group. Systematic deviation (bias) for MH-S was below ±30% when analysed per species and for 25 of 32 agents when analysed per agent. Specific reading instructions were required for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole vs. Streptococcus groups A, B, C and G when tested on MH-S. Inhibition zone diameters on MH-S were not significantly influenced by the three brands of MH investigated. MH-S can be used for DD for all species with EUCAST zone diameter breakpoints on MH-F (except H. influenzae, which does not grow on MH-S). Since MH-F supports growth of more species than MH-S, EUCAST will continue to recommend MH-F as the standard EUCAST medium for disk diffusion testing of fastidious organisms, unless otherwise stated. Updated information is available on the EUCAST website.

title: Experts recommend management strategies for horses during poor air quality.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: To adapt the existing air quality index (AQI) framework to communicate equine health risk and develop practical recommendations for horse care, training, and competitions at increasing levels of air pollution. A 3-round modified Delphi study. 15 expert equine veterinarians contributed, with 11 experts completing 3 rounds. First, experts agreed that both healthy horses and those with underlying health conditions may experience short- and long-term health effects. Second, experts adapted the AQI public health messaging to communicate equine-specific health risk. Third, experts developed practical recommendations for each AQI category, spanning general management, training, and competition decisions. This study utilized the existing AQI framework to develop resources for communicating equine health risk and expert-informed management strategies for each AQI category. Reliance on translational data highlights a critical need for future work prioritizing equine-specific research on health impacts and pollutant thresholds to support refinement of AQI-based guidance. Equine veterinarians are encouraged to widely distribute this equine-specific AQI framework to clients, barn managers, and trainers as a practical framework for informed decision-making to support horse health and welfare during periods of poor air quality.

title: Wolbachia outcompetes mosquito-borne viruses by reprogramming host ATPSβ1-driven ATP metabolism toward symbiotic proliferation.
abstract: Wolbachia endosymbionts confer broad-spectrum resistance to mosquito-borne viruses. While the antiviral metabolites in Wolbachia-Aedes have been identified during viral replication, the core metabolic gene underlying this defense across the entire viral infection cycle remains undefined. Here, we demonstrated for the first time that Wolbachia strongly suppressed the emerging alphavirus Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, extending its known antiviral spectrum. Transcriptomic and functional analyses revealed ATP synthase beta subunit 1 (ATPSβ1) as a key metabolic hub hijacked by both MBV and the symbiont. Without Wolbachia symbiosis, dengue virus and VEEV induced ATPSβ1 to promote viral binding via the viral envelope protein and increased intracellular ATP production for viral replication. Conversely, Wolbachia overrode ATPSβ1-mediated viral binding and redirected ATPSβ1-driven ATP synthesis to fuel its proliferation, strengthening antiviral activity. Pharmacologically, adenosine increased Wolbachia wAlbB density and potently suppressed viral infection in Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus cells. Oligomycin reduced intracellular ATP and inhibited viral infection in Wolbachia-free Ae. aegypti cells. Collectively, Wolbachia repurposes dual-functional ATPSβ1, which governs MBV binding and replication, into a potent antiviral effector through a metabolic tug-of-war over host ATP during symbiont-virus competition. Moreover, we highlight interventions targeting the ATPSβ1-driven metabolism as promising strategies to curb MBV transmission.

title: Serum and uterine fluid extracellular vesicles and prostaglandin E metabolite concentrations during diestrus and early pregnancy in mares.
abstract: Prostaglandins produced by endometrial and conceptus tissues have an established role in maintaining luteal function in early pregnancy and initiating luteolysis during diestrus in mares. The cellular mechanisms controlling the secretion and delivery of prostaglandins have not been fully elucidated. We hypothesized that nanosized lipid bilayer extracellular vesicles (EV) that carry a variety of biological molecules would be involved in these key regulatory processes. Serum and uterine fluid samples were collected from diestrus and pregnant mares on day (D) 10 and D14 post-ovulation, and conceptuses were collected in pregnant mare cycles and cultured for 2-3 h. Extracellular vesicles were isolated using membrane affinity spin columns. Metabolomic EV cargo was assessed using LC-MS/MS, and cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) with immunoblotting. Serum and uterine fluid PGEM and conceptus PGE2 concentrations were compared using ELISA. Prostaglandins were below detection limits in all EV serum and uterine fluid eluates. PGEM concentrations in uterine fluid and serum did not differ between pregnant and diestrus mares at these time points. Day 10 and D14 conceptuses produced PGE2. Serum and uterine fluid EV contained AA and cPLA2. While AA abundance did not differ by reproductive status or day at these time points, uterine fluid EV AA abundance was 83 times higher than serum. Serum and uterine fluid EV carry activatable phospholipases and rate-limiting substrates for prostaglandin production rather than the prostaglandins themselves. High levels of AA in uterine fluid EV are likely important in the local regulation of uterine prostaglandin production.

title: Evaluating a novel automatic feeding device for hay provision in horses: behavioral outcomes in group and individual housing.
abstract: This study evaluated a novel Automatic Feeding Device (AFD) for hay provision in group-housed and individually housed horses. In Phase 1 (P1), behavioral responses to ground hay feeding (Control-Hay) and to hay delivery through the AFD were assessed in three group-housed mares under two conditions: AFD continuously open (O-AFD) and AFD alternating between open and closed periods (OC-AFD). In Phase 2 (P2), four individually housed horses were used to evaluate the behavioral effects of three AFD opening-closing schedules: long opening (LO-OP), medium opening (ME-OP), and short opening (SH-OP). Behavioral data were collected by continuous video recording. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, with treatment as fixed effect and horse as random effect (experimental unit). Principal component analysis was used to explore variability in agonistic behaviors among group-housed horses. In P1, individual differences in foraging activity and agonistic behaviors were observed. Exploratory behaviors increased significantly when the AFD alternated between open and closed periods compared with when it remained open (3.93 ± 3.36 vs. 1.72 ± 3.86 min/h; p = 0.010). Compared with Control-Hay, which resulted in no residual hay, AFD delivery increased residual hay, averaging 3.98 ± 0.77 kg in O-AFD and 4.88 ± 1.00 kg in OC-AFD (p < 0.001). Social hierarchy strongly influenced access to the AFD in group-housed horses. In P2, foraging from the AFD declined progressively from LO-OP and ME-OP to SH-OP (46.91 ± 0.81, 42.80 ± 1.65, and 38.84 ± 0.89 min/h, respectively; p < 0.001). Stress-related behaviors directed toward the AFD were most frequent during SH-OP: pawing occurred up to seven to eight times more often than in LO-OP and ME-OP, while rubbing and teeth or tongue use were approximately two to three times higher. Residual hay increased progressively as access duration decreased (p < 0.001), accompanied by a slight reduction in hay intake rate. Behavioral responses to the AFD were influenced by social dynamics in group-housed horses and feeder access schedule in individually-housed horses. The medium opening interval (40 min open, 20 min closed) appeared to provide the most appropriate balance between regulating hay intake, maintaining feeding behavior and limiting stress-related behaviors.

title: Retrospective serological evidence of exposure to selected equine viruses in horses from Indigenous communities of Costa Rica, 2011.
abstract: Horses are essential for transportation and livelihoods in Indigenous communities of Costa Rica. However, information on their exposure to viral pathogens remains scarce. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional serosurvey using samples collected from horses from four Indigenous communities (Alto Pacuare, Amubre, Paso Marcos, and Vereh) sampled between March and October 2011 (n = 278). Sera were tested in 2014 using commercial immunodiffusion or ELISA assays for antibodies against West Nile virus (WNV), equine herpesviruses 1 and 4 (EHV-1 and EHV-4), influenza A virus, equine arteritis virus (EAV), and equine infectious anemia virus (EIAV). Seroprevalence estimates and Wilson 95% confidence intervals were calculated, and differences among communities were assessed using Pearson's chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, as appropriate. The number of tested sera differed across assays due to sample availability. Serological evidence compatible with WNV exposure was detected in 58.9% (139/236) of horses, with the highest proportion in Amubre (83.3%). EHV-4 showed consistently high seropositivity (91.2%, 125/137), whereas EHV-1 seroprevalence was low (6.6%, 9/137). Antibodies to influenza A virus and EAV were detected at low frequencies (5.1%, 12/237, and 3.0%, 7/236, respectively). EIAV seroprevalence reached 16.6% (35/211), with the highest proportion in Paso Marcos (23.8%). Significant differences among communities were observed for WNV, influenza A virus, and EHV-4 seropositivity. These findings represent historical serological evidence of exposure in 2011 and should not be interpreted as reflecting current viral circulation. Nevertheless, they provide a retrospective baseline for comparison with future surveillance and highlight the value of including underserved Indigenous equine populations in disease-monitoring and prevention programs.

title: Rethinking hyperhomocysteinemia: from causal risk factor to biomarker of glutathione deficiency in chronic diseases.
journal: Critical reviews in clinical laboratory sciences
abstract: Hyperhomocysteinemia (HHcy) is a common metabolic disorder characterized by systemic elevation of the thiol amino acid homocysteine. Although HHcy is recognized as an independent risk factor for cardiovascular and many other chronic diseases, the causes and underlying mechanisms remain unclear despite decades of extensive research. The objective of this review is to critically examine the available literature in order to explore the hypothesis that endogenous glutathione deficiency may represent a primary pathological condition underlying hyperhomocysteinemia. Glutathione (GSH) is a tripeptide composed of the amino acids glycine, cysteine, and glutamate. GSH primarily serves as a master antioxidant, protecting cells from free radicals and playing a crucial role in maintaining redox homeostasis. Beyond its antioxidant properties, GSH plays a crucial role in numerous cellular processes, making it essential for health and for addressing age-related chronic diseases. The review examines into the redox regulation of homocysteine production and the connection between homocysteine and glutathione metabolism, while also addressing methodological aspects of homocysteine and glutathione measurement and the pre‑analytical and analytical challenges associated with their reliable quantification in clinical settings. It also includes a critical analysis of current experimental HHcy models and their relevance for extrapolation to humans. It is concluded that experimental HHcy is confounded by oxidative stress, a pathological condition that results from, contribute to, or be exacerbated by decreased endogenous glutathione levels. A strong negative correlation between homocysteine and glutathione has been demonstrated, and restoration of endogenous glutathione through nutritional interventions is associated with normalization of blood homocysteine. The literature indicates that the same environmental factors that induce oxidative stress and GSH depletion also activate redox‑sensitive enzymes in the methionine cycle and transsulfuration pathway, thereby driving the metabolic shift toward hyperhomocysteinemia. Consequently, these enzymes facilitate the production of homocysteine and its conversion into cysteine, supplying the rate-limiting substrate essential for glutathione biosynthesis. In this context, hyperhomocysteinemia can be considered an indicator of metabolic reprogramming aimed at restoring disrupted redox homeostasis by supporting glutathione biosynthesis, thereby alleviating oxidative stress and its associated pathological changes. The review concludes by outlining the evidence supporting the view that glutathione deficiency, rather than hyperhomocysteinemia, may constitute the primary underlying abnormality in chronic human diseases. The concept of glutathione depletion as a Trojan horse" challenges the prevailing paradigm that attributes disease pathogenesis primarily to hyperhomocysteinemia. Instead, this condition may be better understood as a risk factor for chronic diseases, given that its underlying mechanisms appear to stem from disrupted redox homeostasis and cellular glutathione deficiency. From a practical standpoint, homocysteine measurement offers a simpler and more accessible laboratory surrogate than direct glutathione assessment for screening individuals with potential GSH deficiency. However, fully realizing the clinical utility of this approach will require further research into the molecular mechanisms by which glutathione depletion drives hyperhomocysteinemia. Elucidating these mechanisms could open genuine and cost‑effective opportunities for the prevention and treatment of chronic diseases by shifting the therapeutic focus from homocysteine to glutathione metabolism.

title: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy as a tool for monitoring treatment-related neurofunctional changes in posttraumatic stress disorder and trauma-related symptomatology: a narrative review.
abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in symptom presentation, illness trajectory, and treatment response, highlighting the need for objective approaches capable of monitoring treatment-related neurofunctional changes beyond conventional symptom-based outcomes. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is an increasingly used non-invasive neuroimaging technique that enables repeated assessment of cortical hemodynamics in clinically feasible settings. Although fNIRS has been widely applied to characterize neurofunctional alterations associated with PTSD, its potential role in monitoring longitudinal treatment-related brain changes has not been critically synthesized. A narrative review was conducted using a structured search strategy across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library to identify studies published up to 30 January 2026. Studies were eligible if they included adults with PTSD or clinically significant trauma-related symptomatology and employed repeated NIRS/fNIRS assessments to evaluate neurofunctional changes associated with pharmacological or non-pharmacological therapeutic interventions. Four studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. Across the included studies, the non-pharmacological interventions consisted of trauma-focused psychotherapy, attention-based cognitive training, and equine-assisted services. No eligible longitudinal studies evaluating pharmacological treatments using repeated NIRS/fNIRS assessments were identified. Across studies, treatment was consistently associated with modulation of prefrontal cortical hemodynamic activity, although the direction and magnitude of neurofunctional changes varied according to intervention type, experimental paradigm, and methodological approach. Overall, the available evidence supports the feasibility of repeated fNIRS assessment while highlighting substantial methodological heterogeneity and the limited maturity of the current evidence base. Current evidence suggests that fNIRS represents a promising and clinically feasible approach for monitoring treatment-related neurofunctional changes in PTSD and trauma-related symptomatology, particularly during non-pharmacological interventions targeting prefrontal regulatory processes. Rather than replacing established neuroimaging techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging, fNIRS should be considered a complementary tool that is particularly suitable for repeated assessments in real-world clinical settings. Future research should prioritize adequately powered longitudinal studies, standardized acquisition and analytical protocols, multimodal neuroimaging approaches, and the inclusion of pharmacological treatment trials to determine the potential of fNIRS as a candidate longitudinal neurofunctional biomarker of treatment response. Not applicable.

title: Low-dose histrelin for ovulation induction in mares: a partially randomized crossover pilot study.
abstract: This partially randomized crossover pilot study evaluated reduced doses of histrelin for ovulation induction in mares and compared intramuscular (IM) administration with pharmacopuncture at the Bai-hui and Yan-chi acupoints. Eleven mares were enrolled, of which nine completed all eight protocols and were included in the analyses. The protocols comprised 250 µg histrelin IM (standard dose), 75 µg IM, 25 µg IM, no intervention, saline at Bai-hui, saline at Yan-chi, 25 µg histrelin at Bai-hui, and 25 µg histrelin at Yan-chi. Ovulation was assessed by transrectal ultrasonography at scheduled examinations until detected, with ovulation within 48 h as the primary outcome. Ovulations first detected at 24 h were excluded from the primary analysis. Ovulation within 48 h occurred in 88.9% (8/9) of observations with 250 µg IM, 87.5% (7/8) with 75 µg IM, 87.5% (7/8) with 25 µg IM, 37.5% (3/8) with no intervention, 50.0% (3/6) with saline at Bai-hui, 100% (9/9) with 25 µg histrelin at Bai-hui, 12.5% (1/8) with saline at Yan-chi, and 87.5% (7/8) with 25 µg histrelin at Yan-chi. Exact 95% confidence intervals were wide, reflecting the small sample size. Exploratory pairwise comparisons with the no-intervention protocol were performed without adjustment for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously. The findings provide preliminary evidence that reduced histrelin doses, including 25 µg, may induce ovulation within 48 h in mares. However, this study did not demonstrate an advantage of pharmacopuncture over IM administration of the same reduced dose. Larger, fully randomized studies are required to confirm the efficacy of reduced-dose histrelin and determine whether administration at specific acupoints provides any additional effect.

title: Australian Rotavirus Surveillance Program: Annual Report, 2025.
abstract: This report from the Australian Rotavirus Surveillance Program (ARSP) describes the circulating rotavirus genotypes identified in children and adults during the period 1 January to 31 December 2025. In 2025, the ARSP saw a continuation of a high burden of rotavirus disease in the Australian population. During this period, 2,419 faecal specimens were referred to the National Rotavirus Reference Centre (NRRC) for rotavirus G- and P-genotype analysis; of these samples, 2,288 were confirmed as rotavirus positive. This represents the highest number of referred samples and the highest number of positive samples recorded in a single surveillance year in the NRRC's more than 20-year history. Of the 2,288 samples confirmed rotavirus positive, 2,071 (90.5%) were identified as wildtype rotavirus; 215 (9.4%) were identified as the Rotarix vaccine-like strain; and two G1P[8] samples could not be confirmed as wildtype or vaccine-like due to inadequate sequence quality. The equine-like G3P[8] variant was the dominant genotype nationally (87.7%; n = 1,816/2,071). Other genotypes were identified at low frequencies, including wildtype G1P[8] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071), G2P[4] (2.0%; n = 42/2,071), G3P[8] (2.4%; n = 50/2,071), G8P[8] (0.5%; n = 10/2,071), G9P[4] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071), G9P[8] (2.2%; n = 46/2,071) and G12P[8] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071). Genotype distribution was consistent nationally, with equine-like G3P[8] the dominant genotype in all jurisdictions. Consistent with observations in recent years, a small number of samples with unusual genotypes were identified (3.7%; n = 77/2,071). Of these unusual genotypes, the most frequently detected was equine-like G3P[6] which accounted for 26.0% of unusual samples (n = 20/74) and 1.0% of all positive wildtype samples (n = 20/2,071). The high number of rotavirus positive samples received by the program reflected the notifications for rotavirus disease reported to the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance Service (NNDSS). Across Australia, 9,520 notifications were recorded, which is the second highest annual total reported since rotavirus became nationally notifiable in 2018. Outbreaks were reported in the Northern Territory, Western Australia and Queensland. The ability to monitor the genotypes of rotavirus strains causing disease across ages and jurisdictions provides important data to aid in assessing the performance of the national rotavirus vaccination program and to inform public health interventions during outbreaks. The ARSP also provides important data to monitor annual variations in genotypes circulating in the population. Understanding the diversity of genotypes in circulation and the emergence of variants provides important context for any changes observed in disease epidemiology in the community. The ARSP provides diagnostic laboratories with valuable feedback on laboratory data quality by reporting incidences of wildtype, vaccine-like, and/or false positive rotavirus results.

title: Equine asthma - old disease and new concepts.
abstract: Equine asthma is increasingly recognised as a biologically heterogeneous syndrome in which similar clinical manifestations may arise from distinct molecular mechanisms. Although clinical phenotypes have substantially improved disease classification, increasing evidence indicates that molecular endotypes more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms underlying disease heterogeneity. This review summarises current knowledge regarding the pathophysiological mechanisms of equine asthma, with particular emphasis on inflammatory pathways, molecular endotypes, genetic susceptibility, airway remodelling and emerging neuroimmune interactions. Special attention is given to the transition from phenotype-based disease classification towards mechanism-based endotyping and its potential implications for future diagnostics and targeted therapeutic strategies. The review was based on a comprehensive search of the PubMed and Scopus databases using the terms "equine asthma", "diagnostics", "phenotypes", "endotypes", "genetic background" and "neuroimmune pathophysiology". Following predefined selection criteria, 146 publications were included in the review. Current evidence demonstrates that persistent airway inflammation, structural remodelling, genetic background and neuroimmune signalling interact throughout disease progression and cannot be fully explained by clinical phenotypes alone. Improving our understanding of these biological mechanisms will facilitate more precise disease classification and may provide the foundation for future biomarker-guided diagnosis and precision medicine in equine asthma.

title: Barriers to Australian veterinary students choosing an equine career.
abstract: The equine veterinary profession is experiencing a global recruitment and retention crisis with fewer graduates entering equine practice. We aimed to investigate perceived and actual barriers to Australian veterinary students' considering an equine veterinary career. A mixed methods design was used. The study population consisted of veterinary students from seven universities in Australia. An online survey was distributed that comprised demographic, Likert-scale and open-ended questions and covered themes of equine experience, perceptions of clients, salary, Higher Education Contribution Scheme debt, and perceptions of workplace culture. Descriptive data analysis was performed. Subsequently, students were invited to participate in Zoom interviews to discuss their experiences. Interviews were transcribed and thematically analysed in NVivo. There were 306 online survey responses, of which 239 were complete. Eight Zoom interviews were conducted. Key concerns about equine practice were difficult clients (81%), workplace culture (60%), work-life balance (53%) and long working hours (14%). The perception that one must be 'horsey' to become an equine veterinarian was a dominant theme. Limited early exposure to horses and restricted hands-on opportunities during extramural studies were significant barriers. Recommendations from students included improving clinic culture, supporting 'non-horsey' students, promoting positive equine placements, and providing realistic career pathways. Addressing cultural attitudes, enhancing student equine exposure and improving work-life balance are critical to attracting and retaining graduates in equine practice. Collaborative action between universities, clinics and industry bodies is essential for a sustainable equine veterinary workforce.

title: Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Predicting Breeding Values of Key Performance Traits in Iranian Crossbred (Thoroughbred × Turkmen) Racehorses.
abstract: Accurate prediction of breeding values (BVs) is fundamental to genetic improvement in racehorses. Although single-trait mixed models (STM), typically implemented using BLUP-based procedures, remain the standard framework for genetic evaluation, machine learning (ML) methods offer a flexible, data-driven approach for learning complex relationships among phenotypic, environmental, and pedigree-derived information. These capabilities have encouraged researchers to explore the application of ML methods for predicting breeding values. This study compared the performance of 13 ML algorithms for predicting estimated breeding values (EBVs) of Race Completion Time (RCT), Rank at the End of Competition (REC), and Average Speed (AS) in Iranian crossbred racehorses. A total of 55,070 race records from 5,296 horses were analyzed. Reference EBVs were estimated using single-trait mixed models (STM) fitted by maximum likelihood in Wombat. Thirteen ML algorithms, including linear regression models, tree-based ensembles, boosting methods, and artificial neural networks (ANNs), were trained using 75% of the data and evaluated on the remaining 25%. Predictive performance was assessed using accuracy, correlation, mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), bias, and dispersion. All ML models outperformed the conventional STM across the three traits. ANN consistently achieved the highest predictive performance, with accuracies of 0.63, 0.72, and 0.56 and correlations of 75%, 86%, and 71% for RCT, REC, and AS, respectively. XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting and Random Forest also showed strong predictive ability, whereas linear models and distance-based methods exhibited comparatively lower performance. Prediction bias remained close to zero, and dispersion coefficients were generally close to unity across ML models. Machine learning, particularly ANN and boosting-based algorithms, substantially improved EBV prediction compared with the conventional STM. These findings demonstrate the potential of ML as a complementary tool for accelerating routine genetic evaluation and supporting more reliable selection decisions in horse breeding programs.

title: Medical Therapies for the Treatment of Osteoarthritis in the Horse - 20 years later….
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a debilitating joint disease, characterized by a degenerative catabolic cascade resulting in detrimental changes to all aspects of the joint including the irreversible destruction of articular cartilage. In 2006, a narrative review by Goodrich and Nixon outlined the available treatments for the medical management of OA; however, since that time substantial progress has been made. In recent years the therapeutic options for veterinarians managing horses with OA has increased significantly with a multitude of products available on the market. While many of the conventional treatments remain in clinical use, ongoing research continues to refine their application and evaluate their efficacy. Since their introduction, orthobiologic therapeutics have undergone extensive development, resulting in the emergence of numerous allogenic and autologous therapeutics. Similarly, cellular based therapies have advanced considerably. Overall, these advancements reflect a broader shift in treatment from those aimed predominantly at symptom management to interventions designed to modify the OA disease process. This narrative review follows up on the past 20 years of progress, outlining current evidence-based recommendations to provide a comprehensive guide for clinicians selecting therapeutic agents to treat horses with OA.

title: Equine-Assisted Learning and Social-Emotional Competence in Higher Education: An Exploratory Study of Emerging Adults' Experiences.
journal: The Journal of adolescent health : official publication of the Society for Adolescent Medicine
abstract: Equine-assisted learning (EAL) is an experiential educational approach that engages learners in structured human-horse activities to support character development, interpersonal growth, and life skills. Social-emotional learning (SEL) is increasingly recognized as an important aspect of student development, supporting both wellbeing and academic success. Although much studies have explored how horses may support human health and wellbeing, limited research has explored how undergraduate students experience EAL in relation to SEL within non-Western higher education contexts. An exploratory study was conducted to examine undergraduate students' experiences of participating in an 8-week EAL program at a private Malaysian institution. Fifteen participants (ages 18-24; 73.3% male, 26.7% female) engaged in structured experiential sessions involving guided human-horse interactions. In-depth, semistructured interviews were conducted. The qualitative data were analyzed using an inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes were identified: (1) emotional learning through human-horse interactions, (2) interpersonal engagement through shared activities, and (3) transfer and application of learning. This study suggests that EAL may support SEL processes in higher education, while highlighting the need for further research to examine its effectiveness across diverse settings.

title: Pulled-up race outcomes as welfare-relevant surveillance indicators in United States Steeplechase horses, 2023-2025.
abstract: Pulled-up race outcomes are routinely recorded but are nonspecific, potentially reflecting fatigue, poor performance, footing, rider judgment, suspected injury, or physiological compromise. We evaluated their association with subsequent participation disruption in United States steeplechase horses. National Steeplechase Association Race Results Reports from 2023 to 2025 were analyzed retrospectively at the horse-start level. Outcomes were time to the next later-date start, ≥60-day interruption, ≥183-day absence, and no recorded later-date start. Cox models were stratified by race type with horse-clustered robust covariance; binary outcomes used horse-clustered generalized estimating equations. Sensitivity analyses excluded November starts because racing is seasonal from March through November. Among 3,070 starts by 710 horses, 367 (11.95%) were pulled up, involving 277 horses (39.0%). No later-date start was recorded after 37.6% of pulled-up and 21.2% of non-pulled-up starts. Among returners, median time to the next start was 42 versus 35 days; Kaplan-Meier medians for all starts were 148 versus 45 days. Pulled-up status was associated with a lower recorded return rate (hazard ratio 0.589, 95% confidence interval 0.515-0.675). Race-type-adjusted odds ratios were 2.10 (1.67-2.64) for ≥60-day interruption and 2.36 (1.80-3.10) for ≥183-day absence. Associations persisted after excluding November starts. Pulled-up outcomes were associated with participation disruption, although clinical reasons were unavailable. They may help prioritize follow-up and longitudinal surveillance but cannot replace veterinary examination or clinical records.

title: The Impact of Systemic Treatment With Flunixin Meglumine on the Two Antiproteases Alpha-2-Macroglobulin (A2M) and Alpha-1-Antitrypsin (A1AT) in Equine Plasma and Platelet-Rich Fibrin (PRF).
abstract: To evaluate the effect of flunixin meglumine, a systemic non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), on the antiproteases, A2M and A1AT, in equine plasma and PRF. A prospective cross-sectional study. Plasma, solid PRF, and liquid PRF were collected from a control-group that included healthy horses not treated with NSAIDs within the last 3 months. The NSAID-group were ophthalmology patients with no systemic inflammatory disease, and all received a full dose of flunixin meglumine (1.1 mg/kg BID PO or IV) for three or more days prior to collection. Samples were collected and prepared using a standardized protocol for plasma and PRF preparation. Concentrations of A2M and A1AT were analyzed with ELISA kits. Statistical analysis with Mann-Whitney U tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests was performed using significance set at p 0.05). Plasma had a significantly higher amount of A2M compared to solid and liquid PRF (both p < 0.001). Solid PRF had the highest concentration of A1AT and was significantly higher when compared to liquid PRF (p < 0.001), but not when compared to plasma (p = 0.071). The systemic NSAID, flunixin meglumine, does not appear to significantly alter antiprotease concentrations in equine plasma or PRF. Although PRF should not be used as a replacement for plasma, solid PRF may be a good adjunctive therapy for the treatment of keratomalacia due to its high A1AT concentration.
